sec.title: Background
sec.p: MORPHEUS-UC (NCT03869190) is a signal-seeking, global, phase Ib/II, open-label, multicenter, randomized, umbrella study in patients with platinum-treated locally advanced or metastatic urothelial carcinoma (mUC). Patients were randomly assigned to one of seven atezolizumab (anti-programmed death-ligand 1)-based treatment combinations or atezolizumab monotherapy. We report efficacy and safety results for atezolizumab + sacituzumab govitecan (trophoblast cell surface antigen-2–directed antibody conjugate) versus atezolizumab alone.

sec.title: Patients and methods
sec.p: Eligible patients were checkpoint inhibitor-naïve and experienced disease progression or recurrence during or after ≤1 platinum-containing regimen. Primary endpoints were investigator-assessed objective response rate (ORR) and safety. Secondary efficacy endpoints included investigator-assessed progression-free survival (PFS), duration of response, disease control rate, and overall survival (OS).

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Fifteen patients received atezolizumab + sacituzumab govitecan; 30 received atezolizumab alone. The best confirmed ORR was 6.7% with atezolizumab + sacituzumab govitecan and 27.6% with atezolizumab. No improvement in ORR, PFS, or OS was seen with the addition of sacituzumab govitecan to atezolizumab. Most frequent treatment-related adverse events (TRAEs) were anemia, neutropenia, pruritus, nausea, and alopecia with atezolizumab + sacituzumab govitecan, and pruritus, decreased appetite, rash, and fatigue with atezolizumab. No grade 5 TRAEs occurred.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: The atezolizumab + sacituzumab govitecan efficacy and safety results suggest limited rationale for further development of this combination in platinum-experienced patients with locally advanced or mUC.

list-item.p: No additive benefit in ORR, PFS, or OS was seen with atezo + SG versus atezo alone.
The safety of atezo + SG was consistent with the known risks of each individual study treatment component.
The atezo + SG data do not support its further development in platinum-experienced patients with locally advanced or mUC.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Patients with locally advanced or metastatic urothelial carcinoma (mUC) used to receive platinum-based chemotherapy as standard-of-care (SOC) first-line (1L) treatment, if eligible.1 Treatment paradigms over time have evolved and checkpoint inhibitors (CPIs) combined with enfortumab vedotin or cisplatin-based chemotherapy are now considered the SOC for 1L treatment.2, 3, 4 However, treatment options remain limited for patients whose disease progresses after 1L treatment.5

MORPHEUS-UC (NCT03869190) is a signal-seeking, global, phase Ib/II, open-label, multicenter, randomized, umbrella study in patients with platinum-treated locally advanced or mUC.6 Patients were randomly assigned to one of seven atezolizumab (anti-programmed death-ligand 1 [PD-(L)1] CPI)-based treatment combinations or the atezolizumab monotherapy control. Combinations with atezolizumab are being explored because despite not having statistically significant overall survival (OS) benefit at the primary analysis (median follow-up: 11.1 months) in the IMvigor211 study, updated OS analysis demonstrated long-term durable remission (median follow-up: 33 months) in platinum-experienced patients with locally advanced or mUC.7,8 Further, at both the primary and updated analyses, the safety profile of atezolizumab alone was favorable compared with chemotherapy. The European Medicines Agency approved the use of atezolizumab as a treatment option for patients with locally advanced or mUC after platinum chemotherapy treatment or who are cisplatin-ineligible and whose tumors have a ≥5% PD-L1 expression.9 Sacituzumab govitecan, a trophoblast cell surface antigen 2-directed antibody conjugate, has shown promising activity in this patient population both alone and in combination with a CPI.10, 11, 12 As part of the MORPHEUS-UC study, the combination of atezolizumab with sacituzumab govitecan was evaluated to determine whether there is a synergistic antitumor effect from this combination regimen. Here, we report efficacy and safety results for atezolizumab + sacitzumab govitecan versus atezolizumab alone in platinum-experienced patients with locally advanced or mUC.

sec.title: Patients and methods
sec.p: The MORPHEUS-UC study design, including clinical data from other atezolizumab combinations, has been previously published.6 The protocol was approved by institutional review boards at each site.6 Study conduct was in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. Enrolled patients provided written informed consent.

Briefly, eligible CPI-naïve patients had locally advanced (stage T4b, any N; or any T, N2-N3) or mUC (M1, stage IV) and were required to have experienced disease progression or recurrence during or after treatment with ≤1 platinum-containing regimen. Atezolizumab 1200 mg was administered intravenously on day 1 of each 21-day cycle (experimental and control arms). Sacituzumab govitecan 10 mg/kg was administered intravenously on day 1 and day 8 of each 21-day cycle (experimental arm). For management of drug-related toxicities, no dose modification for atezolizumab was permitted in this study. The dose of sacituzumab govitecan could be reduced by 2.5 mg/kg up to two times and sacituzumab govitecan was discontinued if further dose reductions were deemed necessary. Re-escalation of sacituzumab govitecan dosage was not permitted.

The primary efficacy endpoint was investigator-assessed objective response rate (ORR) per the RECIST version 1.1. Key secondary efficacy endpoints included investigator-assessed progression-free survival (PFS), duration of response (DOR), and disease control rate (DCR), all per RECIST 1.1, and OS. Confirmed ORR was the proportion of patients with a complete or partial response on two consecutive occasions ≥4 weeks apart. PFS was defined as the time from randomization to the first occurrence of disease progression or death from any cause, whichever occurred first. The time from the first occurrence of a documented objective response to disease progression or death from any cause, whichever occurred first, was defined as DOR. DCR included patients with stable disease for ≥12 weeks or a complete or partial response. OS was defined as the time from randomization to death from any cause. Safety was evaluated according to the National Cancer Institute Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events, v4.0.

This study was not designed to make explicit power and type I error considerations for a hypothesis test. Instead, the study was designed to obtain preliminary data, including data on efficacy, safety, and biomarkers. ORR and DCR were calculated for each arm, along with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) using the Clopper–Pearson exact method. Median DOR, PFS, and OS were estimated using the Kaplan–Meier method, with 95% CIs constructed using the Brookmeyer and Crowley method. Decisions regarding the further development of the combination treatment were informed by calculating the Bayesian posterior probability of the true difference in ORR between the experimental and control arms.

sec.title: Study population
sec.p: Across six countries (France, Greece, Spain, Republic of Korea, UK, and USA) and 14 study sites, 45 patients were enrolled and randomly assigned (n = 15, atezolizumab + sacituzumab govitecan; n = 30, atezolizumab). Baseline characteristics are shown in Supplementary Table S1, available at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.esmoop.2026.108303. As of the clinical cut-off date (27 October 2023), the median duration of survival follow-up was 13.2 months for the atezolizumab + sacituzumab govitecan arm and 17.8 months for the atezolizumab arm. All patients in the atezolizumab + sacituzumab govitecan arm and 26 of 30 (89.7%) receiving atezolizumab had discontinued treatment (Supplementary Table S2, available at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.esmoop.2026.108303).

sec.title: Clinical activity
sec.p:
The confirmed ORR was 6.7% (95% CI 0.17% to 31.95%) in the atezolizumab + sacituzumab govitecan arm compared with 27.6% (95% CI 12.73% to 47.24%) in the atezolizumab arm (Table 1). sec.title: Safety
sec.p:
Treatment exposure and safety are summarized in Table 2. Overall, all patients, regardless of treatment arm, experienced at least one adverse event (AE) of any grade. Grade 3/4 AEs occurred in 11 patients (73.3%) in the atezolizumab + sacituzumab govitecan arm and 9 patients (31.0%) in the atezolizumab arm. Grade 5 AEs were reported in one patient (6.7%) in the atezolizumab + sacituzumab govitecan arm, which was due to sepsis and was considered unrelated to study drugs. There were no grade 5 AEs in the atezolizumab arm. AEs that led to discontinuation of any study treatment were reported in three patients (20.0%) in the atezolizumab + sacituzumab govitecan arm and in no patients in the atezolizumab arm. Two patients (13.3%) in the atezolizumab + sacituzumab govitecan arm experienced an AE that led to dose reduction of sacituzumab govitecan (diarrhea and stomatitis, each occurring in one patient).Table 2

Treatment-related AEs occurred in 13 patients (86.7%) in the atezolizumab + sacituzumab govitecan arm and in 19 patients (65.5%) in the atezolizumab arm. A higher incidence of anemia, neutropenia, nausea, alopecia, diarrhea, and vomiting was observed in the atezolizumab + sacituzumab govitecan arm than in the atezolizumab arm, where these events were rare or did not occur (Supplementary Table S3, available at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.esmoop.2026.108303). Serious AEs related to any study treatment were reported in five patients (33.3%) in the atezolizumab + sacituzumab govitecan arm and in one patient (3.4%) in the atezolizumab arm (Table 2). Two patients (13.3%) experienced febrile neutropenia classified as a serious AE related to any study treatment in the atezolizumab + sacituzumab govitecan arm. Both events occurred during the first cycle of treatment. Primary prophylaxis with granulocyte colony-stimulating factor was not given to either patient. For one patient, study drugs were withdrawn due to sepsis after febrile neutropenia, whereas in the other patient, prophylactic granulocyte colony-stimulating factor treatment was given in the subsequent cycles.

Immune-related AEs of specific concern, called AEs of special interest related to atezolizumab, are included in Supplementary Table S4, available at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.esmoop.2026.108303. The most common AEs of special interest were rash (33.3%) and hepatitis (laboratory abnormalities, 26.7%) in the atezolizumab + sacituzumab arm and rash (24.1%) and hypothyroidism (13.8%) in the atezolizumab arm.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Overall, efficacy was not improved with the addition of sacituzumab govitecan to atezolizumab. Here, the ORR with atezolizumab + sacituzumab govitecan was 6.7%, which was numerically lower than the ORR seen in previous studies that evaluated the study drugs individually. For example, cohort 3 of the TROPHY-U-01 study reported an ORR of 41% for sacituzumab govitecan alone in a patient population that was CPI-naïve and had disease progression after 1L platinum-based chemotherapy.12 In comparison, the atezolizumab monotherapy ORR in this report was 27.6%, which was consistent with previous MORPHEUS-UC data (clinical cut-off: 8 April 2022).6 Consistent with the ORR results, DCR, PFS, and OS were not improved with the addition of sacituzumab govitecan to atezolizumab.

The AE profile of atezolizumab + sacituzumab govitecan was generally consistent with data from each agent, with no new or unexpected safety concerns. treatment-related AEs occurred at a higher incidence in the atezolizumab + sacituzumab govitecan arm when compared with atezolizumab alone (86.7% compared with 65.5%). Additionally, there was a numerically higher rate of treatment discontinuation and dose modification/interruption due to AEs and lower treatment exposure in the combination arm compared with atezolizumab monotherapy. The higher toxicity seen in the atezolizumab + sacituzumab govitecan arm compared with the atezolizumab arm may have contributed to the poorer efficacy outcomes observed in this study.

The MORPHEUS-UC study had several limitations, including the very small number of patients enrolled, the lack of stratification during randomization, and the lack of a prespecified statistical plan. Furthermore, there was an imbalance in baseline sites of disease. Additionally, the control arm used is no longer the SOC. However, a key strength of MORPHEUS-UC is that the signal-seeking design can quickly examine potential new treatments, as was done here.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: The atezolizumab + sacituzumab govitecan efficacy and safety results suggest limited rationale for further development of this combination in platinum-experienced patients with locally advanced or mUC.

sec.p: Qualified researchers can request access to individual patient-level clinical data through a data request platform. At the time of this writing, this request platform is Vivli (https://vivli.org/ourmember/roche/). For up-to-date details of Roche’s Global Policy on the Sharing of Clinical Information and how to request access to related clinical study documents, see https://go.roche.com/data_sharing.
